doc.title: Wendell Harrison interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 17, 2022 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Concert production, Tribe magazine and founding the label
summary: With Phil Ranelin he produced concerts at the Detroit Institute of Arts and taught, which led to the Tribe magazine and record label amid unrest, and independent distributors.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: No, well anyway she wanted me to meet a young lady that she, in her mind was a real credible lady and she thought that we could get married and make a family together, you know have kids and whatnot. Never did happen. But it happened where she was very instrumental in managing and administrating some of my gigs and my career. And when I started working and teaching here in Detroit Phil Ranelin and myself, Phil came from Indianapolis, and we put together a production company where we was producing shows at the art institute, it was a museum, the Detroit Institute of Arts. This was a museum. And we produced concerts every three months you know. And then I started teaching here at the same time, teaching jazz studies at a place called Metro Arts. So we produced these shows. It was a program book that we got together and we had people that was working, at the Harrison Association that was working and selling ads and whatnot and tickets ads in the program guide, it was a program guide and they would sell ads. And the revenue off of that money would actually support the musicians, promotion, and renting of the venues. Very successful at that particular time because people wanted to do things. You know people wanted to, especially the black community was coming together, under Nixon, it was really coming together at that particular time because people were very distraught about the war in Vietnam and the economy. The economy was down at that particular time. People didn’t have jobs you know, social unrest. Riots was breaking out everywhere you know. People was restless. So anyway, so people would come together, we had artists, photographers, writers, musicians, we came together and formed an organization that presented concerts and stuff every quarter, and that became a foundation for the magazine, the publication magazine called Tribe. And it was a social, economic issue, as well as politics and art. And it was very successful. Then we took some of that money and put it into a record label called Tribe. That was successful because we had independents, independent distributors that no longer wanted to like distribute company product, like Columbia, Atlantic and the whole thing. And they wanted to have their own economy and distributing what they wanted to distribute. You know sometimes these distributors were actually
Columbia would only want you to distribute their product. Case in point, just thinking about this, the people that recorded us were

Atlantic Records in the distribution were into sales and selling product to distributors and whatnot and they wanted to record independent artists. So they recorded us you know. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
